q: A feature vector is [3, -4, 12]. Which pair correctly gives its L1 norm and its max norm?
options: 19 and 12
13 and 12
19 and 4
13 and 4
explanation: L1 adds the absolute values: 3 + 4 + 12 = 19. The max norm is the largest absolute entry, 12. (13 is the L2 norm, √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169.) For every vector, max norm ≤ L2 ≤ L1.

q: For a = [2, -1, 0] and b = [4, 3, 5], what is a · b, and what does its sign tell you?
options: 11; the vectors point almost exactly the same way
5; they point roughly the same way (angle under 90°)
-5; they point roughly opposite ways
8; the vectors are exactly perpendicular
explanation: a · b = 2·4 + (-1)·3 + 0·5 = 5. Because a · b = ‖a‖ ‖b‖ cos θ, a positive value means the angle is under 90°. Here cos θ = 5 / (√5 · √50) ≈ 0.32, so they are only weakly aligned; a dot product of 0 would mean perpendicular.

q: A has shape (4 × 3) and B has shape (3 × 2). Which statement about the product AB is correct?
options: It is invalid because the outer sizes 4 and 2 differ
It is valid and has shape (3 × 3)
It is valid only after transposing B first
It is valid and has shape (4 × 2)
explanation: The inner sizes must match (A's 3 columns, B's 3 rows) and the result takes the outer sizes, (4 × 2). Each of the 8 cells is a 3-term dot product, so the cost is about 2·4·3·2 = 48 FLOPs. B·A would be a different (3 × 3) matrix.

q: A 2 × 2 matrix has rows [2, 5] and [1, 3]. What does its determinant say about invertibility?
options: det = 1, so the matrix is invertible
det = 0, so the matrix is singular
det = 11, so the matrix is singular
det = -1, so the matrix has no inverse
explanation: For a 2 × 2 matrix det = ad − bc = 2·3 − 5·1 = 1. Any non-zero determinant means the matrix does not squish space flat, so an inverse exists; |det| = 1 means areas keep their size. A determinant of 0 (rows that are multiples of each other) would mean singular.

q: A linear layer Y = X·Wᵀ + b (the PyTorch nn.Linear layout) takes a batch X of shape (64, 512) and has W of shape (256, 512). The layer above hands back G = ∂L/∂Y. What are the shapes of ∂L/∂W and ∂L/∂b?
options: (64, 512) from G·W, and (64,) from summing G over the features
(512, 256) from Xᵀ·G, and (256,) taken from the first row of G
(64, 256), the same as G, and (256,) averaged over the features
(256, 512) from Gᵀ·X, and (256,) from summing G over the batch rows
explanation: Every gradient has the shape of the thing it belongs to. ∂L/∂W = Gᵀ·X: (256, 64) @ (64, 512) = (256, 512), and the matrix multiply adds up the 64 examples for free. b was added to every row, so its gradient sums G over the rows: (256,). G·W = (64, 512) is ∂L/∂X, the error signal passed to the layer below. Taking only row 0 of G for the bias is a silent bug, because (256,) still matches (256,).

q: For A·v = λ·v, which interpretation is most precise?
options: A rotates every vector through an angle of exactly λ radians
λ must equal zero whenever the matrix A is invertible
v is any vector at all whose length happens to equal λ
v keeps its direction; A only stretches it by the factor λ
explanation: An eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches (or flips, if λ is negative), and λ is the stretch factor. For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], v = [1, 1] gives A·v = [3, 3] = 3·v, while [1, 0] is turned into [2, 1], so it is not an eigenvector. An invertible matrix has no zero eigenvalue.

q: PCA finds covariance eigenvalues 9, 3 and 0.5. About what fraction of the variance do the top two principal components explain?
explanation: Each eigenvalue is the variance along its component, so the share is (9 + 3) / (9 + 3 + 0.5) = 12 / 12.5 = 96%. PC1 alone explains 9 / 12.5 = 72%. Standardise features first when units differ, or the feature with the biggest numbers dominates PC1.

q: In the SVD A = U Σ Vᵀ, which piece holds the stretch amounts (singular values), sorted from largest to smallest?
options: U
Vᵀ
A⁻¹
Σ
explanation: U and V are orthogonal (rotations, possibly with a mirror flip) and Σ is the diagonal matrix of singular values. Keeping only the top k gives the best possible rank-k copy of A (Eckart–Young), with an error made of exactly the singular values dropped.

q: In scaled dot-product attention, why are the scores Q·Kᵀ divided by √d_k before the softmax?
options: To keep the score variance near 1 so the softmax stays soft
To make Q, K and V share identical learned projection weights
To shrink the score matrix from (n × n) down to (n × d_k)
To replace the softmax with a cheaper linear normalisation
explanation: With unit-variance entries, q · k sums d_k products and has variance d_k, a spread of about ±8 at d_k = 64. Softmax of numbers that far apart is nearly one-hot, and its gradients are near zero. Dividing by √d_k brings the variance back to 1; it acts like a fixed temperature.

q: A decoder-only transformer uses causal masking. Which entries of the n × n score matrix are set to −∞, and when?
options: The diagonal (each token itself), after the softmax
The lower triangle (earlier tokens), before the softmax
The upper triangle (later tokens), before the softmax
The upper triangle (later tokens), after the softmax
explanation: Each position may attend only to itself and earlier positions, so the upper triangle (future tokens) is set to −∞ before the softmax, which then gives those positions weight exactly 0. Masking after the softmax would leave rows that no longer add up to 1.

q: With d_model = 768 split equally across h = 12 heads, what is d_k per head, and how many weights do the query, key, value and output projections hold together (no biases)?
options: 64 per head, and 4 × 768² ≈ 2.36 million in total
64 per head, and 12 × 4 × 768² ≈ 28.3 million
768 per head, and 4 × 768² ≈ 2.36 million in total
32 per head, and 4 × 64² ≈ 16 thousand in total
explanation: d_k = d_model / h = 768 / 12 = 64. The four projections are each 768 × 768 in total, so 4 × 768² = 2,359,296 weights — the same for any number of heads, because the heads only split those matrices into slices.

q: At the flat point (0, 0) of f(x, y) = x² + 3xy + 2y², the Hessian is [[2, 3], [3, 4]], with eigenvalues of about 6.16 and −0.16. What kind of point is it?
options: A minimum, because both diagonal entries are positive
A maximum, because the determinant is negative
A saddle, because the eigenvalues have mixed signs
Undecidable without computing the third derivatives
explanation: At a flat point, all-positive eigenvalues mean a bowl (minimum), all-negative a hilltop (maximum), mixed signs a saddle. The 2 × 2 shortcut agrees: det = 2·4 − 3·3 = −1 < 0. Stepping to (1, 0) goes uphill (f = 1) but stepping to (1, −0.72) goes downhill (f = −0.1232). Positive diagonal entries alone do not make a minimum.

q: For f(x, y) = x² + 3xy + y², what is ∂f/∂y at the point (x = 2, y = 1)?
explanation: Freeze x and differentiate in y: ∂f/∂y = 3x + 2y, which is 6 + 2 = 8 at (2, 1). (7 is ∂f/∂x = 2x + 3y at the same point.)

q: For the chain a = 2x − 1, b = a³, L = 5b, what is dL/dx at x = 2?
explanation: At x = 2, a = 3. Multiply the local slopes: dL/db = 5, db/da = 3a² = 27, da/dx = 2, so dL/dx = 5 · 27 · 2 = 270. Backpropagation is exactly this multiplication, done from the loss backwards.

q: You gradient-check f(x) = x³ at x = 2 (true slope 12) with a nudge h = 0.1: the one-sided difference gives 12.61 and the central difference 12.01. If you shrink h to 0.01, what happens to the two errors?
options: Both errors shrink about 10×
One-sided shrinks about 10×, central about 100×
One-sided shrinks about 100×, central about 10×
Both stay the same; only rounding noise changes
explanation: The one-sided error shrinks like h (0.61 → 0.06), while the central difference (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / 2h shrinks like h² (0.01 → 0.0001). That is why gradient checks use the central version, with h around 1e-5 to 1e-6 in float64 — a far smaller h lets rounding noise take over.

q: For f(x, y) = x² + y², start at (5, −1) with learning rate 0.1. Where does one gradient-descent step land?
explanation: ∇f = [2x, 2y] = [10, −2]. Step against it: (5, −1) − 0.1 · [10, −2] = (4, −0.8). On this bowl every step multiplies each coordinate by 1 − 2·0.1 = 0.8. (6.0, −1.2) is where a step uphill, along +∇f, would land.

q: A function maps 3 inputs to 2 outputs. What is the shape of its Jacobian, and what does entry (i, j) mean?
options: 3 × 2; the curvature between inputs i and j
2 × 2; the determinant of the output transformation
2 × 3; how output i changes when input j is nudged
3 × 3; the probability of output class j for input i
explanation: The Jacobian has one row per output and one column per input, so 2 × 3, with entry (i, j) = ∂F_i/∂x_j. Backprop never builds it in full; it computes a vector–Jacobian product vᵀJ (reverse mode), which is cheap when there is one output, the loss.

q: Why don't deep-learning frameworks build and invert the full Hessian of a large network?
options: It only exists for categorical variables, not continuous weights
It always points uphill, so it can never help an optimizer descend
It is identical to the gradient in any network that uses ReLU
Its n² entries (10¹² for a million weights) are far too many to store
explanation: A million weights give a 10¹²-entry Hessian (about 4 TB in FP32), and inverting it costs about n³ operations. Practical methods use Hessian–vector products, which never build H, or cheap approximations (Sophia's diagonal estimate, Shampoo/SOAP's per-matrix preconditioners). Adam's per-weight scale is not the Hessian.

q: In the chapter's tiny network (h = 1.1, a = ReLU(h), o = w2·a + b2), why does dL/dh equal dL/da?
options: The squared-error loss always has a derivative of exactly 1
The ReLU's slope is 1 on its positive side, and h > 0
The output weight w2 becomes zero during the backward pass
The bias gradient cancels out the activation's derivative
explanation: dL/dh = dL/da · ReLU′(h), and ReLU′(h) = 1 when h > 0, so the upstream gradient (0.678 here) passes through unchanged. With x = −2, h = −0.9 < 0, the slope is 0, and w1 and b1 get no gradient for that input.

q: A classifier's true accuracy is 90%. On a 1,000-image test it scores 91.2%. Treating each image as an independent right/wrong trial, is this evidence that it beats 90%?
options: Yes: 912 is 12 above the expected 900, which is beyond normal luck
Yes: on 1,000 images any gain over one point is significant
No: with an SD of about 9.5, 912 or more happens 11% of the time
No: accuracy counts follow a Poisson law, so tests are meaningless
explanation: The number correct is Binomial(n = 1,000, p = 0.9): mean 900, SD √(1000 · 0.9 · 0.1) ≈ 9.5. A score of 912 is only 1.26 SD above the mean, and P(912 or more) ≈ 11%, so a truly 90% model scores this high fairly often by luck alone.

q: Using C(4, 2) · p² · (1 − p)², what is the probability of exactly 2 heads in 4 fair coin flips?
explanation: C(4, 2) = 6 orderings, each with probability 0.5⁴ = 1/16, so 6/16 = 0.375. The binomial mean is np = 2 heads and the variance np(1 − p) = 1.

q: Heights are roughly Gaussian with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. About 95% of people fall in which range?
options: 162 to 178 cm
154 to 186 cm
146 to 194 cm
170 to 186 cm
explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule puts about 95% within μ ± 2σ = 170 ± 16, so 154 to 186 cm (exactly 95% lies within ±1.96σ). 162 to 178 cm is ±1σ (68%) and 146 to 194 cm is ±3σ (99.7%).

q: An LLM outputs one probability for every token in its vocabulary (50,257 tokens for GPT-2, 128,256 for Llama 3). Which distribution is that?
options: Bernoulli
Poisson
Gaussian
Categorical
explanation: A categorical distribution gives probabilities to K options that add up to 1, which is exactly what softmax produces. Bernoulli is one yes/no trial, Poisson counts events in a time window, and a Gaussian is a continuous bell curve.

q: A game pays 0 USD with probability 0.7 and 10 USD with probability 0.3. What is the expected payout per play?
options: 3 USD
7 USD
10 USD
0.21 USD
explanation: E[X] = Σ x · P(x) = 0 · 0.7 + 10 · 0.3 = 3 USD. It is the long-run average per play, not a payout you can actually receive on any single play.

q: Values 2, 4, 6 and 8 are equally likely. What is their variance, dividing by n as the population formula does?
explanation: The mean is 5; the squared deviations are 9, 1, 1 and 9, whose average is 20 / 4 = 5. Dividing by n − 1 instead (the sample estimate, the default of pandas and np.cov) gives 6.67, so pass ddof explicitly.

q: Two features have covariance 12 and standard deviations 3 and 4. What is Pearson's correlation r?
explanation: r = Cov(X, Y) / (σX · σY) = 12 / (3 · 4) = 1: a perfect positive straight-line relationship, as for a feature duplicated in different units. Covariance changes with the units; r does not.

q: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated. What is the best explanation?
options: Eating ice cream directly raises the risk of drowning
A confounder, hot weather, drives both of them up
Correlation only works for categorical labels, so it is invalid here
A positive correlation means one series duplicates the other
explanation: Correlation measures association, not cause: both rise in hot weather, a confounder. Remember too that r only measures straight-line links — y = x² on x = −2 … 2 has r = 0 despite y being fully determined by x.

q: Asha labels 60% of your images with a 2% error rate; Ravi labels 40% with a 5% error rate. What fraction of all labels is wrong, and what share of the wrong labels are Ravi's?
options: 3.5% wrong; Ravi's share is 40%
3.2% wrong; Ravi's share is 62.5%
7.0% wrong; Ravi's share is 71.4%
3.2% wrong; Ravi's share is 40%
explanation: Law of total probability: 0.6 · 0.02 + 0.4 · 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. Ravi's share of the errors is 0.020 / 0.032 = 62.5% — Bayes' theorem, with the total probability as its denominator. He did 40% of the labelling but 62.5% of the mistakes.

q: A disease has 2% prevalence; the test has 90% sensitivity and a 10% false-positive rate. A patient tests positive. What is P(disease | positive)?
options: About 15.5%
About 20.0%
About 77.6%
About 90.0%
explanation: P(positive) = 0.9 · 0.02 + 0.1 · 0.98 = 0.018 + 0.098 = 0.116 (law of total probability). Bayes: 0.018 / 0.116 ≈ 15.5%. False positives from the 98% healthy majority outnumber true positives more than 5 to 1; answering 90% (the sensitivity) is the base-rate fallacy.

q: The true distribution has two peaks, but your model can only form one bump. Minimising which KL direction makes the model spread over both peaks?
options: Reverse KL, D_KL(Q‖P), because it punishes Q > 0 where P ≈ 0
Forward KL, D_KL(P‖Q), because it punishes Q ≈ 0 where P > 0
Either one, because KL divergence is symmetric in P and Q
Neither; only a symmetric distance can cover several peaks
explanation: Forward KL (truth first) explodes wherever the model gives near-zero probability to something real, so it is mode-covering — what cross-entropy / MLE training minimises. Reverse KL is mode-seeking. For P = [0.45, 0.05, 0.05, 0.45], forward KL is 0.368 for an even spread vs 0.703 for a one-peak model; reverse KL flips the verdict (0.511 vs 0.431).

q: You draw two cards from a 52-card deck without replacement, and the first is an ace. What is the probability the second is also an ace, and are the two draws independent?
options: 4/52 ≈ 7.7%; yes, each draw is independent
1/221 ≈ 0.45%; no, both cards must be aces
3/51 ≈ 5.9%; no, the first draw changed the deck
3/52 ≈ 5.8%; yes, one ace is simply gone
explanation: Given the first ace, the world shrinks to 51 cards with 3 aces: P(B | A) = 3/51 ≈ 5.9%, lower than 4/52 ≈ 7.7%, so the draws are dependent. 1/221 = 4/52 × 3/51 is P(both aces), from the always-true multiplication rule P(A) · P(B | A).

q: The spread of an average of N independent draws is σ/√N. If σ = 12 and N = 36, what is it, and how much data would halve it?
options: 2; four times the data (N = 144) halves it
0.33; twice the data (N = 72) halves it
6; twice the data (N = 72) halves it
2; twice the data (N = 72) halves it
explanation: SE = 12 / √36 = 12 / 6 = 2. Because of the square root, halving it takes 4× the data: 12 / √144 = 1. That is why eval error bars and mini-batch noise shrink only slowly as N grows.

q: Why does the chapter connect mini-batch gradient descent to the Central Limit Theorem?
options: A mini-batch gradient is an average, so its noise shrinks like 1/√B
Each per-example gradient must itself be exactly Gaussian
The weights become normally distributed after every update
A large enough batch makes the loss surface convex
explanation: The mini-batch gradient averages B per-example gradients, so it points the right way on average and its noise falls like 1/√B: 64× the batch gives 1/8 of the noise. The per-example gradients themselves need not be Gaussian.

q: A coin lands heads 8 times in 10 flips. Which p does maximum likelihood estimation choose?
explanation: Setting the derivative of 8 log p + 2 log(1 − p) to zero gives 8/p = 2/(1 − p), so p̂ = 8/10 = 0.8, the observed fraction. Adding a Beta(2, 2) prior (MAP) would pull it towards 0.5: (8 + 1)/(10 + 2) = 0.75.

q: LLM pre-training maximises Σ log P(next token | previous tokens, θ). Minimising which quantity is equivalent?
options: Σ P(next token | previous tokens, θ), without the log
Σ log θ, summed over every parameter of the model
‖θ‖₂, the L2 norm of all the model's weights
Σ −log P(next token | previous tokens, θ)
explanation: Maximising the log-likelihood is the same as minimising its negative, and −log P(correct token) is the cross-entropy loss. So training an LLM with cross-entropy is maximum likelihood estimation.

q: A model comparison reports p = 0.03. What does that p-value mean?
options: Data this extreme would occur 3% of the time if the null were true
There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is actually true
The measured improvement is worth 3% in practical business terms
Only 3% of the test examples were predicted correctly by the model
explanation: A p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H0), computed assuming the null is true. It is not P(H0 | data) — that needs a prior and Bayes' theorem — and it says nothing about how large or important the effect is.

q: Model A gets 920/1000 correct and model B 935/1000, on separate random samples. A two-proportion z-test gives z = 1.29 and p = 0.196, with α = 0.05. What is the right conclusion?
options: Model B is proven to be the better model
The 1.5-point gain is statistically significant
Not enough evidence: the gain could be noise
The null hypothesis has a 19.6% chance of being true
explanation: 0.196 > 0.05, so the gap is not significant: its 95% interval, −0.8 to +3.8 points, includes 0. That means 'not proven', not 'no effect' — about 4,700 examples per model would give 80% power, and the same gap on 10,000 each gives p ≈ 0.00004.

q: In the decomposition expected test error = Bias² + Variance + σ², which term can no model remove?
options: Bias²
Variance
Model capacity
The label noise σ²
explanation: σ² is randomness in the labels themselves, so it sets the performance floor. Bias and variance are traded off through model size and regularisation. (In the chapter's SGD run the loss never drops below about 0.25 = 0.5², the label-noise variance.)

q: Which pattern best signals high variance (overfitting)?
options: High training error and high test error
Low training error but high test error
Equal training and test error near zero
High label noise and nothing else
explanation: A high-variance model memorises the noise in its training set, so training error is low while test error stays high. High bias (underfitting) shows high error on both.

q: You estimate a true value f = 1 from the mean of 5 labels with noise variance σ² = 1. Why can the shrunk estimate 0.833 × mean have lower test error than the unbiased mean?
options: Shrinking removes the label noise σ² from the test error
Unbiased estimators always have the highest possible variance
Shrinking lowers bias, and lower bias always means lower error
It adds bias² of 0.028 but cuts variance from 0.200 to 0.139
explanation: Bias² = (1 − 0.833)² = 0.028 and variance = 0.833² × 1/5 = 0.139, so the total is 0.028 + 0.139 + 1 = 1.167, versus 0 + 0.200 + 1 = 1.200 for the plain mean. A little bias buys a bigger variance cut — the case for regularisation in one line. The noise term σ² never moves.

q: Gradient descent on L(θ) = θ², starting at θ = 10, uses learning rate 1.1. What happens?
options: It lands exactly on the minimum after one step
It bounces between +10 and −10 forever
It converges slowly because the step is too small
Each step multiplies θ by −1.2, so it diverges
explanation: The slope is 2θ, so each step multiplies θ by 1 − 2·lr. lr = 1.1 gives −1.2: θ flips sign and grows, reaching about 383 after 20 steps. lr = 0.5 lands exactly (factor 0) and lr = 1.0 bounces forever (factor −1); in general a bowl of curvature h needs lr < 2/h.

q: Momentum updates v(t) = 0.9 · v(t−1) + 0.1 · g(t). If v(t−1) = 2 and the current gradient g(t) = 3, what is v(t)?
explanation: v = 0.9 · 2 + 0.1 · 3 = 1.8 + 0.3 = 2.1: 90% of the old direction plus 10% of the new gradient. 4.8 comes from PyTorch's form without the 0.1 (v = 0.9v + g), whose velocity is 10× larger and so pairs with a 10× smaller learning rate.

q: Per weight, what do Adam's two running averages m and v track?
options: The weight's mean value and its validation loss
The mean gradient and the mean squared gradient
BatchNorm's mean and variance used at inference
The weight's L1 and L2 penalty terms
explanation: m is the running mean of the gradient (the direction, like momentum) and v the running mean of the squared gradient — an uncentred second moment, so √v is the typical size of the gradient, not its spread. The step lr · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) moves each weight by about lr, whatever its gradient's scale.

q: Adam (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) starts m and v at zero. Without bias correction, how would its very first update compare with the corrected one?
options: About 10× too small, since m is only 10% of the first gradient
Exactly the same, because the two zero starts cancel out
About 1,000× too small, since v is only 0.1% of the first g²
About 3× too large: v is 1,000× too small, under a square root
explanation: At t = 1, m = 0.1g is 10× too small but v = 0.001g² is 1,000× too small, and v sits under a square root: 0.1 / √0.001 ≈ 3.16× too large. Dividing by 1 − β^t fixes it, so the corrected first step is exactly lr (g = 0.2 gives a step of 0.001). For a steady gradient the uncorrected overshoot peaks near 6.6× around step 12.

q: What makes AdamW different from Adam with an L2 penalty added to the loss?
options: AdamW removes the first-moment estimate entirely
AdamW normalises each mini-batch before every update
AdamW switches to plain SGD steps after warmup ends
AdamW shrinks the weights directly, outside the adaptive step
explanation: With L2 in the loss, the decay term passes through Adam's denominator, so weights with a large gradient history are barely decayed. AdamW subtracts lr · λ · θ separately — the same proportional shrink for every weight. With lr = 0.001 and λ = 0.1 each weight shrinks 0.01% per step, to about 0.819 of its size after 2,000 steps if nothing pushes back.

q: Weights w = [0.2, −0.4], λ = 0.5 and a data loss of 1.0. What is the total loss with an L1 penalty λ · Σ|wᵢ|?
explanation: L1 penalty = 0.5 × (0.2 + 0.4) = 0.3, so the total is 1.3. With an L2 penalty λ · Σwᵢ² it would be 0.5 × (0.04 + 0.16) = 0.1, total 1.1 — squaring makes small weights cost far less under L2.

q: With standardised, uncorrelated features and λ = 0.1, the unregularised weights are [0.6, 0.05, −0.3]. What do L1 (λ · Σ|w|) and L2 (λ · Σw²) return?
explanation: L1 soft-thresholds: subtract λ from each size and stop at 0, so 0.05 (≤ λ) becomes exactly 0 — automatic feature selection. L2 divides every weight by 1 + 2λ = 1.2: everything shrinks and nothing reaches 0.

q: Which geometric picture explains why L1 gives exact zeros and L2 does not?
options: L1's constraint region is a circle with no corners
L1 uses a Gaussian prior centred away from zero
L1's diamond has corners sitting on the axes
L1's pull fades away as weights approach zero
explanation: Growing loss contours usually touch the L1 diamond first at a corner, and the corners lie on the axes, where one weight is exactly 0. L2's circle has no corners, so weights shrink but stay non-zero. A pull that fades near zero (2λw) is L2's; L1 pulls with a constant ±λ. L1 matches a Laplace prior, L2 a Gaussian.

q: BatchNorm and LayerNorm differ in which numbers supply the mean and variance. Which pairing is correct?
options: BatchNorm: one sample's features; LayerNorm: one feature across the batch
BatchNorm: one feature across the batch; LayerNorm: one sample's features
BatchNorm: the time steps only; LayerNorm: the labels only
BatchNorm: the weights; LayerNorm: the gradients
explanation: BatchNorm normalises each feature down the batch column; LayerNorm normalises each sample (token) across its own features. So LayerNorm does not depend on batch-mates and suits variable-length sequences in Transformers.

q: Why does LayerNorm behave identically during training and inference, unlike BatchNorm?
options: It uses running averages accumulated from earlier batches
It depends on the labels rather than on the activations
Its statistics come from each sample's own features
It has no learnable scale or shift parameters at all
explanation: LayerNorm's mean and variance come from one sample's features, so nothing depends on who else is in the batch. BatchNorm uses batch statistics in training and running averages at inference, and its batch mean wobbles at small batch sizes (about ±71% of σ at B = 2).

q: How does RMSNorm differ from LayerNorm?
options: It skips the mean subtraction and divides by the root-mean-square
It normalises each feature across the mini-batch, not each token
It needs running averages of the statistics at inference time
It applies dropout to the input before every normalisation step
explanation: RMSNorm computes y = g · x / RMS(x): no centring and no β, so d learned gains instead of 2d. [3.0, 1.5, 2.0] has RMS 2.25 and becomes [1.33, 0.67, 0.89], whose mean is 0.96, not 0. It ignores a rescaling of the input but not a shift, and it is used by Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek.

q: A language model's average cross-entropy on a test set is 3 bits per token. What is its perplexity?
explanation: Perplexity = 2^(cross-entropy in bits) = e^(cross-entropy in nats), so 2³ = 8: the model is as unsure as if it were picking uniformly among 8 tokens. Compare perplexities only on the same text with the same tokenizer.

q: The true class is class 2 (a one-hot label) and the model gives it probability 0.25. What is the cross-entropy loss?
options: log(4)
explanation: With a one-hot label every other term drops out, leaving −log Q(correct) = −log 0.25 = log 4 ≈ 1.386 nats. Confident mistakes cost the most: probability 0.01 on the right answer costs 4.6 nats.

q: Which relationship links cross-entropy H(P, Q), entropy H(P) and KL divergence?
options: H(P) = H(P, Q) + KL(P‖Q)
KL(P‖Q) = H(P) + H(P, Q)
H(P, Q) = H(P) + KL(P‖Q)
H(P, Q) = KL(P‖Q) − H(P)
explanation: Cross-entropy = entropy + KL. The truth's entropy is fixed, so minimising cross-entropy minimises KL. In the chapter's example both models share H(P) = 1.033 nats, and only the KL part (0.006 vs 1.062) separates the good model from the bad one.

q: Why do RLHF (PPO) and DPO include a KL term to a frozen reference model?
options: To make the attention masks bidirectional during fine-tuning
To keep the tuned model from drifting far from its original behaviour
To replace cross-entropy with ordinary least squares
To compute the determinant of the covariance matrix
explanation: KL measures how far the tuned model has drifted from the reference. PPO adds β · KL(tuned ‖ reference) as a penalty, and DPO builds the same leash into its loss through log-ratios. It keeps helpfulness tuning from erasing what the model already knew.

q: In float64, computing e^1000 returns infinity. Which floating-point problem is this?
options: Cancellation
Underflow
Overflow
Absorption
explanation: Overflow: the true value is too big to represent (float64 tops out near e^709.8). Underflow is the opposite (e^−1000 becomes 0); absorption is a small number vanishing when added to a big one; cancellation is precision lost when subtracting nearly equal numbers.

q: The log-sum-exp trick makes softmax numerically stable by doing what first?
options: Dividing every logit by the vocabulary size
Subtracting the largest logit from every logit
Squaring the logits before exponentiating them
Clipping the probabilities after the softmax
explanation: e^(x − m) = e^x · e^(−m), and the e^(−m) cancels between top and bottom, so the result is unchanged. softmax([1000, 1001, 1002]) becomes softmax([−2, −1, 0]) = [0.090, 0.245, 0.665]: every exponent is ≤ 0, so nothing overflows, and the largest term is e⁰ = 1, so the sum cannot underflow.

q: Logits [2, 1, 0] give the top token 0.665 at temperature T = 1. What happens at T = 0.5 and at T = 2?
options: T = 0.5: top token 0.867, sharper; T = 2: 0.506, flatter
T = 0.5: top token 0.506, flatter; T = 2: 0.867, sharper
Both stay at 0.665; temperature only reorders the tokens
T = 0.5 makes the last token most likely; T = 2 the first
explanation: Softmax(z / T) multiplies every gap between scores by 1/T. T = 0.5 sharpens to [0.867, 0.117, 0.016] (entropy 0.636 bits); T = 2 flattens to [0.506, 0.307, 0.186] (1.472 bits). The ranking never changes, so greedy decoding picks the same token at any T > 0.

q: A weight of 1.0 receives an update of 0.0001. In BF16 the gap between 1 and the next representable number is about 0.0078. What happens, and how does mixed precision handle it?
options: The update is rounded away; keep FP32 master weights for updates
The update is stored exactly, since BF16 matches FP32's precision
The weight overflows to infinity, so switch the run to FP16
The update is doubled, so apply loss scaling to shrink it back
explanation: 0.0001 is far below half the gap after 1, so 1 + 0.0001 rounds back to 1 (absorption) — in FP16 too, whose gap is 0.000977. Mixed precision runs the matrix maths in BF16 or FP16 but applies every update to an FP32 master copy (gap 1.2e-7), where it survives.

q: Which 16-bit format keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits — and so FP32's range — at the cost of coarser rounding, and is the training default on TPUs and A100-or-newer GPUs?
options: FP16
BF16
FP8 E4M3
FP4 E2M1
explanation: BF16 (1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa bits) matches FP32's range, so it almost never overflows and needs no loss scaling, but it keeps only 2–3 decimal digits. FP16 (5 exponent, 10 mantissa bits) is more precise but overflows above 65,504 and flushes tiny gradients to zero.
